analysis.one_liner: Sends families up to $360 per child every month as a fully refundable tax credit.
analysis.headline: The bill sat in the Senate Finance Committee without a hearing, a markup, or any vote for the rest of the session so far.
analysis.plain_summary: The American Family Act would replace today's child tax credit with a larger, fully refundable monthly payment: $300 a month ($3,600 a year) for each child between ages 6 and 17, and $360 a month ($4,320 a year) for each child under 6, plus $500 a year for other dependents. Every family with children would get it, including families that owe little or no federal income tax, with the amount phasing down only for households earning above roughly $150,000 (couples) or $112,500 (others). Payments would arrive by bank transfer each month, and parents of newborns would be enrolled automatically. The bill was introduced by Senator Michael Bennet with 44 cosponsors — every one a Democrat or independent — and was sent to the Senate Finance Committee, which has not taken it up.
analysis.who_benefits: Families with children — especially low- and middle-income families — gain a monthly cash payment of $300 per child age 6–17 and $360 per child under 6, fully refundable so that families with no income tax liability receive the full amount, with larger payments for infants. Caregivers who are not parents (such as grandparents raising grandchildren) can qualify, and parents of newborns are enrolled automatically.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Families with children, especially low-income ones

how_it_helps.text: Creates a monthly child tax credit of $300 per child age 6–17 and $360 per child under 6, paid in cash each month and fully refundable, meaning families with little or no federal income tax owed still receive the full amount.
Makes the benefit available to low-income families in full — unlike the current child tax credit, which is limited by how much tax a family owes — and provides larger amounts for infants.
Adjusts the amounts for inflation and phases the credit down only above $150,000 for couples and $112,500 for others, shielding middle- and low-income families from any reduction.

Includes a $500 credit for other dependents and rules protecting advance payments from garnishment and offsets, and provides grace periods and hardship relief so families are not forced to repay for months they briefly lost eligibility.

analysis.who_pays: The federal government bears the cost of the new payments, which are financed through the tax code — the bill text includes no offset, so the cost would fall on federal borrowing or future revenue decisions. Higher-income households lose some or all of the current child credit value as the new credit phases down above $150,000 (couples) or $112,500 (others).
analysis.who_pays_short: Federal taxpayers; higher earners lose some credit

drawbacks.text: The credit phases down once a household's income exceeds $150,000 (married) or $112,500 (others), and further above $400,000/$300,000, so higher-income families receive less or nothing — a cost to those families and a limit on the benefit's universality.

Monthly advance payments must be reconciled at tax time: families whose income rises or whose eligibility changes during the year can owe back part of the advance payments, which can be an unwelcome surprise bill for households on tight budgets.
The bill sets no revenue source in its text; the added federal cost of a large refundable credit would add to deficits or require offsets not included in this bill.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The main benefit is large and direct: a fully refundable, monthly child benefit would cut child poverty substantially and reach families regardless of tax liability, and it includes real anti-fraud and identification safeguards. The main costs are fiscal (the bill text sets no revenue offset in the provided text) and design trade-offs: phasing the credit down at high incomes and conditioning eligibility on care are reasonable limits, but monthly advance payments can require some families to repay money at tax time if their circumstances change. The bill never advanced far enough for those design questions to be debated in committee.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, which never acted on it, so it has had no hearing, no vote, and no path to becoming law so far.

narrative.text: Introduced in the Senate on April 9, 2025, and read twice before being referred to the Committee on Finance.
No further action has been taken: no hearing, no committee markup, and no floor vote appear in the action history.

All 44 cosponsors are Democrats or allied independents; no Republican signed on, and with 47 senators in the Democratic caucus the bill's sponsors would need Republican support to reach the 60 votes typically required to advance most legislation in the Senate.
The bill text would end the existing child tax credit structure for years after 2024 and replace it with the new monthly credit.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, the outcome preserves the tax code as it is: families with little income tax liability continue to receive a smaller, less accessible child tax credit, and no new cost is imposed on taxpayers. Families with children, especially low-income ones, are the ones losing out while the bill sits.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The tax code stays as it is; families gain nothing yet

for.name: Sen. Michael Bennet
for.what_they_did: Introduced the American Family Act to create a refundable monthly child tax credit.

for.name: 42 Democratic senators and 2 independents
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors, including Sen. Wyden (Finance chair) and Sen. Schumer (majority leader).

for.name: Senate Committee on Finance
for.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and has taken no action — no hearing, markup, or vote is recorded.

sides.party_line_note: All 44 cosponsors are Democrats or independents; no Republican cosponsored, and the bill has not advanced in the Republican-held Senate.

industries.industry: Higher-income households and tax filers above the phase-down thresholds
industries.note: A fully refundable child credit financed through the tax code is a large transfer toward families with children paid for by taxpayers generally; households above $150,000/$112,500 lose some or all of the credit relative to a universal benefit.

industries.industry: Tax preparation and financial services firms
industries.note: Monthly federal payments and an IRS online portal could reduce demand for refund-advance products and paid preparer services for low-income families, while payment processing and identity-verification rules create some compliance work.

analysis.trajectory: With no Republican cosponsors, no Finance Committee action, and a Senate that generally requires 60 votes to move most bills, the likely path is that the bill remains in committee and expires at the end of the 119th Congress unless it is attached to a larger tax or reconciliation package.
